# Details on the algorithm
`r params$description`

## Implementation in our analysis

<ul>
  <li>The <em>CIMLR</em> package in R allows the user to only select the number of neighbors for the diffusion steps (argument ``k`` in ``CIMLR()``). However, parameters $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\delta$, $\lambda$, $r$ and the number of iterations ``NITER`` are preset. The hyperparameters $\gamma$ and $\rho$ are not explicitly defined in the code, but their effects may be realized through the kernel weighting adjustments in the internal function ``umkl()`` (for $\rho$) and eigenvalue decomposition in ``eig1()`` (for $\gamma$). Nevertheless, these parameters have been empirically set by the authors and tuning for all of them would be computationally intense. </li>
  <li>Our input consists of four continuous modalities (normalized RNA-seq, normalized CNV, normalized miRNA and normalized Methylation) and one binary modality (SNP). During kernel construction, the distances between samples and their neighbors ($nn$ closest neighbors; different than $nn$) are squared Euclidean distances (as coded in the internal ``MOVICS:::dist2.cimlr()`` function). We modify this function (along with functions where it is called, namely ``MOVICS:::multiple.kernel.cimlr()`` and ``MOVICS::CIMLR()``) in order to include binary distance calculation, as defined by the ``stats::dist()`` function). The modified functions ``dist2.cimlr_mod2()``, ``multiple.kernel.cimlr_mod()`` and ``CIMLR_mod()`` can be found in the <a href="https://github.com/sionaris/MultiOmicsSurvey/blob/main/Scripts/automated_scripts/custom_functions.R">R script</a> that contains all custom functions we defined in our project's repository: ``Scripts/automated_scripts/custom_functions.R``.</li>
  <li>We set ``no.dim = NA``, which forces $t$-SNE to project its input to $C$ dimensions (controlled by the ``c`` argument in ``CIMLR_mod()``) and cluster them into $C$ clusters. We set ``c = 2``, which is the optimal number of multi-omic clusters determined through the MOVICS baeline analysis. </li>
  <li>In order to pick a value for $nn'$, we compared the final $S$ for each $nn'$ value we used. Results from pairwise matrix comparisons by measuring Pearson correlations and Frobenius norms, revealed major differences in final pairwise similarities across samples for each value of $nn'$. Low Pearson values and higher Frobenius norms were observed. We proceeded by assessing variance, IQR, skewness and kurtosis in the matrices (see [Hyperparameters and tuning](#hyperparams-tuning)), in order to pick the similarity matrix $S$ we would eventually proceed with. This approach examines the degree of separation that can be achieved in the high-dimensional space, not the embedded space produced by $t$-SNE. It is not guaranteed that better separation in $S$ will ensure better separation in the embedded space. However, instead of assessing separation in the embedded space, we prefer to assess it as this was achieved after iterations of the CIMLR algorithm using the original input.</li>
  <li>After obtaining the final embeddings that are used as input for $t$-SNE, we used them as input to reference-based Monte-Carlo consensus clustering for $k$-means, using the [<em>M3C</em> package](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-58766-1) in R. This algorithm first generates data from null (i.e. from a single cluster) reference distributions which preserve the correlation structure of the real data ($t$-SNE output) and then applies the $k$-means method to different randomly chosen subsamples (resamplings) of the real data. After $k$-means clustering is completed for a number of resampling iterations, results are aggregated in a consensus matrix which is then hierarchically clustered into $C$ groups to produce the final output. The package also incorporates statistical hypothesis testing for whether the identified number of clusters is statistically significant, using $C = 1$ as the null hypothesis.</li>
  <li>We set the number of Monte Carlo iterations, which affects how many times the algorithm simulates datasets to generate a null distribution of stability scores, to 100. The number of resampling iterations for both reference and real data, which controls how many times the consensus clustering is repeated to evaluate stability, is set to 250. We chose the $k$-means clustering algorithm as the original CIMLR does. The objective function, which influences how the stability of clusters is evaluated, was left as the default ``entropy``. Additionally, we set the maximum number of clusters (``maxK``), which limits the algorithm to testing only $K = 2$. The default method (the Monte Carlo simulation method) was applied for clustering stability estimation. The reference data generation method, which determines how the null distribution is constructed, was also left at the default, ``ref_method = 'reverse-pca'``. Other parameters, such as ``pItem`` (the fraction of points resampled in each iteration) were left at their defaults (``pItem = 0.8``).</li>
</ul>

## Differential Gene Expression Analysis (DGEA)
DGEA is performed in order to compare the expression of the two identified consensus subtypes using the __limma__ package.

In order to identify subtype-specific markers, we find the markers that are up-regulated in `r paste0(params$algorithm, 1)` vs. all other clusters and the ones which are down-regulated in `r paste0(params$algorithm, 1)` vs. all other clusters etc.

In this procedure, the most differentially expressed genes sorted by __log2FoldChange__ (actual differential expression value in the case of standardized expression data) are chosen as the biomarkers for each subtype (200 biomarkers for each subtype by default; Here we set 200 -> 100 markers). These biomarkers should pass the significance threshold (e.g., nominal $p$-value < 0.05 and adjusted $p$-value < 0.05) and must not overlap with any biomarkers identified for other subtypes.

<b>Up-regulated markers</b>

## Fraction of Genome Altered (FGA)
In the case of CNVs, we also generate a plot of the fraction of genome that is altered (FGA) in the samples of each identified subtype. This plot uses original counts of copy number segments as input and applies a custom definition of gain and loss. In our work, we used two approaches in annotating segments in a sample with one of three possible labels: "gain", "loss", and "normal".

In the first, simpler approach, we define gain as a copy number > 2, loss as a copy number < 2, and normal as copy number equal to 2. In the second approach, we use COSMIC criteria to define gain and loss, which also take average ploidy in each sample into account. More specifically, we define five cases:

$$
\text{Status} = 
\begin{cases} 
    \text{gain} & \text{if ploidy} \leq 2.7 \text{ and copy number} \geq 5, \\
    \text{gain} & \text{if ploidy} > 2.7 \text{ and copy number} \geq 9, \\
    \text{loss} & \text{if ploidy} \leq 2.7 \text{ and copy number} = 0, \\
    \text{loss} & \text{if ploidy} > 2.7 \text{ and copy number} < \text{ploidy} - 2.7, \\
    \text{normal} & \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
$$

We modified the MOVICS ``compFGA()`` function, which compares subtypes based on the FGA, FGG, and FGL. The function performs statistical tests to compare the subtypes using either parametric or non-parametric methods, depending on the number of subtypes and the chosen test method. We modified the function to allow for predefined gain/loss/normal annotations.

Mathematically, FGA, FGG, and FGL are defined as:

$$
\text{FGA} = \frac{\sum (\text{bases where classification is "gain" or "loss"})}{\sum (\text{total bases})}
$$

$$
\text{FGG} = \frac{\sum (\text{bases where classification is "gain"})}{\sum (\text{total bases})}
$$

$$
\text{FGL} = \frac{\sum (\text{bases where classification is "loss"})}{\sum (\text{total bases})}
$$

We used original copy number counts and non-parametric tests:

- **Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Non-parametric, 2 subtypes)**: 
    If there are two subtypes, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test is used to compare the values of FGA, FGG, and FGL between the two subtypes.
    
- **Kruskal-Wallis Test (Non-parametric, more than 2 subtypes)**: 
    When there are more than two subtypes, the Kruskal-Wallis test (kruskal.test) is applied. This is a non-parametric version of ANOVA used to detect differences between multiple subtypes. Additionally, pairwise comparisons between subtypes are performed using the Wilcoxon test with the Benjamini-Hochberg p-value adjustment.

In all cases, the function summarizes the FGA, FGG, and FGL values for each subtype and calculates the respective $p$-values to assess statistical significance.

![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/",params$algorithm,"/pdf2png/FGA_barplot_",params$algorithm,"-1.png")`)
![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/",params$algorithm,"/pdf2png/COSMIC_criteria_FGA_barplot_",params$algorithm,"-1.png")`)

## Gene Set Enrichment Analysis

GSEA is carried out using a gene set background which includes all gene sets derived from GO biological processes (``Resources/Pathways/c5.go.bp.v2024.1.Hs.symbols.gmt``) from The Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB, https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/msigdb/index.jsp).

Likewise, these identified specific pathways should pass the significance threshold (e.g., nominal $p$-value < 0.05 and adjusted $p$-value < 0.25; we set the latter to <u>0.05</u>) and must not overlap with any pathways identified for other subtypes. After having the subtype-specific pathways, genes that are inside the pathways are retrieved to calculate a single sample enrichment score by using ``GSVA`` R package. Subsequently, subtype-specific enrichment score will be represented by the mean or median (mean by default) value within the subtype, and will be further visualized by diagonal heatmap.

![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/",params$algorithm,"/pdf2png/upregulated_pathway_heatmap_using_upregulated_pathways-1.png")`)

# Evaluation results
## Nearest Template Prediction (NTP)
MOVICS provides two model-free approaches for subtype prediction in validation cohort. First, MOVICS switches to nearest template prediction ([NTP](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21124904/)) which can be flexibly applied to cross-platform, cross-species, and multiclass predictions without any optimization of analysis parameters.

Here cosine similarity is used to compare external samples to class templates (here we use the up-regulated genes in the form of a binary matrix with two columns: "cluster #" where an entry is 1 if the gene is up-regulated in the cluster # or -1 otherwise). The nearest class for each sample is determined by the smallest distance (converted from cosine similarity here). Each sample's result includes the nearest class prediction, the distance to all templates, and the p-value of the prediction.

The function randomly permutes the sample labels multiple times (here ``nPerm = 10000``) to generate a null distribution of similarity scores between samples and class templates. For each observed sample-to-template distance, the function compares it against the null distribution to calculate a $p$-value. This $p$-value indicates the likelihood that the observed match could have occurred by chance. The $p$-values are adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) method to control for multiple hypothesis testing, ensuring robust statistical inference.

![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/",params$algorithm,"/pdf2png/ntp_expr_up_heatmap_transNEO-1.png")`)
![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/",params$algorithm,"/pdf2png/ntp_expr_down_heatmap_transNEO-1.png")`)

Results on the comparisons of `r params$evaluation_source` clinical variables with respect to the predicted consensus subtypes are summarised in [this file](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/",params$algorithm,"/transNEO_Summary_of_clinical_variables.txt")`). Grade before NAT administration, number of chemotherapy cycles and the number of adjuvant HER2 treatment were also tested using the Jonckheere-Terpstra test for ordered differences. See conclusions for significant results.

## Partition Around Medoids (PAM)

To be specific, ``runPAM()`` first trains a partition around medoids (PAM) classifier in the discovery (training) cohort (i.e., `r params$data_source`) to predict the subtype for patients in the external validation (testing) cohort (i.e., `r params$evaluation_source`), and each sample in the validation cohort was assigned to a subtype label whose centroid had the highest Pearson correlation with the sample. Finally, the [in-group proportion (IGP)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16613834/) statistic (the proportion of samples within a cluster that were classified into the same cluster upon random permutation of the data) is estimated to evaluate the similarity and reproducibility of the acquired subtypes between discovery and validation cohorts (i.e. are the clusters identified in `r params$data_source` reproducible in `r params$evaluation_source` after label permutation).

## Subtype agreement
Here we examine how similar the consensus multi-omic clustering labels are to other labels relative to breast cancer.

MOVICS provides function of ``compAgree()`` to calculate four statistics: Rand Index (RI), Adjusted Mutual Information (AMI), Jaccard Index (JI), and Fowlkes-Mallows (FM); all these measurements range from 0 to 1 and the larger the value is, the more similar the compared groups are. 

![](`r paste0(params$home,"/Results/single_algorithm/",params$algorithm,"/pdf2png/Classification_agreement-1.png")`)

## Comparison to MOVICS `r params$algorithm`

In MOVICS, the `r params$algorithm` algorithm is run by default with $nn' = 10$ and using only Euclidean distances.

<b>ARI:</b> `r params$ARI_to_MOVICS_CIMLR`
<b>NMI:</b> `r params$NMI_to_MOVICS_CIMLR`

# Conclusions
<ol>
  <li>The identified `r params$algorithm` subtypes are associated with <b>vital status, history of neoadjuvant treatment, PR status, ER status, HER2 status (not confirmed in bar charts), ER and PR cell level percentages, and histological type</b>.</li>
  <li>The identified CIMLR subtypes are **NOT** similar to the MOVICS CIMLR subtypes (<b>ARI:</b> `r params$ARI_to_MOVICS_CIMLR`, <b>NMI:</b> `r params$NMI_to_MOVICS_CIMLR`).</li>
  <li>There are significant differences in the <b>fraction of genome lost</b> of the two subtypes. </li>
  <li>Differential expression analysis of CIMLR clusters indicates that <b>the true number of clusters may be 3</b>; CIMLR1 may be split in two clusters, one of which is predominantly consisting of ER+ samples, and the other one has a noticeable proprotion of ER- samples.
  <li>CIMLR2 samples have (on average) <b>up-regulated mitosis and Th17 pathways</b> compared to CIMLR1, which demonstrates increased <b>extracellular matrix activity</b>.</li>
  <li>CIMLR1 has a high proportion of <em>PIK3CA</em> <b>mutations</b> and CIMLR2 has a high proportion of <em>TP53</em> <b>mutations</b>. CIMLR1 has a relatively high ratio of <em>CDH1</em> mutations too.</li>
  <li>In terms of <b>drug sensitivity</b>, CIMLR1 seems to be more sensitive to <b>sorafenib and lapatinib</b> compared to CIMLR2, and less sensitive to <b>doxorubicin and cisplatin</b>.</li>
  <li>Predicted CIMLR subtypes on the transNEO cohort are associated with lymph node status at diagnosis, ER status, grade, <b>pCR</b> (see table below), PAM50, iC10, RCB score, STAT1.gsva score, GGI.gsva score, ESC.gsva score, TMB and HRD.sum. </li>
</ol>

```{r resp_table, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE}
# Create the data frame
table_data <- table(params$transNEO_var2comp[[params$algorithm]], params$transNEO_var2comp$pCR.RD)

# Calculate percentages
percentage_data <- 100 * prop.table(table_data, 1)

# Create a function to format the output as "count (percentage%)"
format_response <- function(counts, percentages) {
  paste0(counts, " (", round(percentages, 1), "%)")
}

# Initialize an empty data frame
data_resp <- data.frame(Response = c("pCR", "Residual Disease"))

# Loop over the groups to fill the data frame
for (alg_group in rownames(table_data)) {
  pcr_counts <- table_data[alg_group, "pCR"]
  rd_counts <- table_data[alg_group, "Residual Disease"]
  
  pcr_percent <- percentage_data[alg_group, "pCR"]
  rd_percent <- percentage_data[alg_group, "Residual Disease"]
  
  # Add the formatted values to the data frame
  data_resp[[alg_group]] <- c(
    format_response(pcr_counts, pcr_percent),
    format_response(rd_counts, rd_percent)
  )
}

# Print the table using knitr::kable
knitr::kable(data_resp, caption = paste0("Response rates across transNEO ", params$algorithm, " subtypes"))
```
